scribe_response.text: Is there a celebration you remember especially well? The celebration I remember best is the street party for the Jubilee in nineteen seventy-seven. We were living on Ash Grove in Headingley then, in a house with a bay window. Helen was two, and she wore a red paper crown that kept, kept slipping over her uh eyes. Weeks beforehand, Missus Garside from number nine formed a committee and appointed herself chairman. She called a meeting in her front room and served sherry in egg cups. Everyone got a job, and mine was to do the food. Alan was asked to draw a um plan of the tables because he was the draughtsman. He spent three evenings with a ruler and a set square and produced something worthy of a cathedral. The tables came from the church hall and the school, and none of them matched. We covered them with bedsheets and fastened the corners with clothes pegs. Bunting went up on the Saturday, hundreds of little red, white and blue flags strung between the um lamp posts. A man from the shop lent us a ladder and held it. The forecast was dreadful, but on the morning itself the sun came out. By noon um the whole street was carrying plates, jugs and folding chairs into the road. What happened next? There were sausage rolls, egg sandwiches, trifles in um glass bowls and a jelly shaped like a rabbit. I made forty fairy cakes and iced them in red and blue with a silver ball on each. Old Mister Ackroyd from number four sat at the head of the table in his medals and an overcoat. He said he had been to three coronations and a hundred funerals, and he preferred parties. The children ran races, and the woman blew a whistle for them. The egg and um spoon um race was won by a boy who had cheated, and nobody minded. Then came the tug of war, the men against the women, and we won. Alan fell flat on his back in the gutter, and the whole street cheered. A man from the pub brought a piano on a cart, and we sang until our throats hurt. I remember Missus Garside conducting with a wooden spoon um during the hymns. In mid afternoon the clouds rolled in, and big warm drops of rain began to fall. Nobody went home, because the food was still on the tables and the singing was too uh good. We dragged the tables together under the railway bridge at the end of the street. The bridge echoed, and our singing sounded like a cathedral uh choir. Can you tell me more about that? Helen fell asleep on a pile of coats with jelly on her chin. As evening came, someone lit a fire in an old oil drum, and we toasted marshmallows. The teenagers danced to a record player on a, a very long cable from Missus Garside's window. Alan danced with me, and he was terrible, as, as always, but he um held on tightly. I remember the smell of wet pavement, woodsmoke and cold tea. By eleven the children were asleep on laps, and the grown-ups were quiet. We stacked the chairs and washed the cups in a bowl on the pavement. Mister Ackroyd shook my hand uh and said it was the finest day since the war ended. The next morning the street looked tired, with um wet flags and a um shoe lying there. We found a hundred pennies in the gutter, which had fallen from someone's pockets. Missus Garside collected them and gave them um to the hospital in the name of the street. That was the first time I realised how a street can become a family. We stayed in that house for twenty years, and we never had another party like it. Whenever I see bunting now, I can smell the rain and hear that piano, piano.
